questions.question: Why should AI Cost and Value Economics be taught as a workflow instead of only as tool awareness?
options: Because a low per-call model price is on its own enough proof that a business case holds
Because teams need shared signals, controls, and decision rules they can apply to real work
Because a claimed time saving per employee already counts as value before adoption is measured
Because integration, review, and support effort can be estimated once and never revisited
questions.explanation: The lesson is built around reusable operating artifacts — shared signals, controls, and decision rules — not the idea that a low token price proves a case, that a claimed time saving is value before adoption, or that integration and review effort can be estimated once and left alone.

questions.question: In the lesson's opening example, why did the approved assistant's promised savings never show up in operations metrics?
options: The token bill for the assistant turned out to be far larger than the original estimate suggested
The license cost of the assistant was renegotiated upward halfway through the rollout period
Operations had no monitoring in place at all, so the gain did happen but stayed invisible in the metrics
Adoption stayed low, reviewers still checked every output, and integration work ran higher than planned
questions.explanation: The lesson's opening example approves the project because model cost looks small, then value never materializes: adoption is low, reviewers still check every output, and integration work exceeds the estimate — not a token bill overrun, a renegotiated license, or a missing monitoring setup.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce for AI Cost and Value Economics?
options: A finished business case ready to submit for funding without review, because one plausible output is sufficient production evidence
A ranked plan with category, score, priority, controls, and rationale
A single cost-of-ownership figure with no assumptions attached
An invoice reconciling token spend against the license budget
questions.explanation: The lesson's Python artifact outputs a ranked plan — category, score, priority, controls, and rationale — not a submit-ready business case, a bare cost-of-ownership figure, or a token-spend invoice.

questions.question: Which control belongs to the lesson design?
options: Counting the promised time saving as realized value before any baseline is measured
A baseline metric, so the team can tell whether the operations number actually moved
Leaving the adoption-rate assumption out of the log because the pilot felt convincing
Treating a single low token price as the sensitivity range for the whole business case
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls include a baseline metric — the reference point that shows whether the operations number actually moved — the opposite of counting promised savings as realized value, leaving adoption assumptions out of the log, or collapsing a sensitivity range into one token price.

questions.question: When should a scenario become a launch-gate discussion rather than a casual awareness exercise?
options: When impact, uncertainty, and matched risk signals such as adoption rate are all running high
Only when the license cost of the tool crosses a specific annual spending threshold agreed upfront
Only when the value case is presented to leadership rather than to the delivery team
Never — a weak value case can always be corrected at the next budget review round
questions.explanation: High-impact, uncertain, risk-heavy value cases need a launch gate regardless of the license spend, who the case is presented to, or whether another budget review is already scheduled.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the output template?
options: To formally replace the benefits owner's accountability for the value case after funding
To keep shaky cost assumptions out of sight of the people making the funding call
To create a reusable worksheet or prompt that teams can keep applying after the course ends
To automatically generate completion certificates for participants once the workshop ends, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
questions.explanation: The output template is a value case calculator and assumption log teams keep applying after the course — not a substitute for the benefits owner's accountability, a way to hide cost assumptions, or an automatic certificate generator.
